Vehicles
A commitment to transition to plug-in hybrid or electric
vehicles  has  been  put in place,  aiming  in particular  to
conv ert La Banque  Postale’s entire internal fleet by 2030.
In addition to the deployment of this vehicle policy,
dedicated support is planned for eligible employees.
The 2030  target is to reduce the carbon impact by
1,223  tCO₂e compared to  the 2021 baseline year
(2,806  tCO₂e),  by:
•continuing  to deploy the vehicle policy for the
La Banque Postale SA scope (reduction of 841 tCO₂e by
2030)  with, in particular, the continuation of eco-driving
training , as well as the possibility of extending the fixed
compensatory  allowance  to company vehicles;
•deploying  a vehicle policy for the subsidiaries concerned
(reduction  of 383 tCO₂e by  2030).
La  Banque  Postale is continuing  to replace the vehicle
fleet  to reach 100% electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles in
the service  and  company vehicle fleet.
Travel
Sustainable mobility initiatives favour  public transport for
business 
travel and offer incentives such as the sustainable
mobility  package for commuting. Teleworking is also
encouraged.
The 2030  target is to reduce the carbon impact by
6,566  tCO₂e compared to the 2021 baseline year
(26,264   tCO₂e). This  target is  accompanied by  a modal
shift target of 17% (i.e. 16,224 single-occupancy vehicles
targeted),  and  is broken  down  as follows:
•the use of public transport (target of 2,298 tCO₂e reduction
in CO2 by 2030) by including park and ride subscription
fees 
in the "soft mobility pass", or by launching discussions
on the terms  of additional  financial incentives;
•developing  the use of  active modes (target  of 591 tCO₂e
reduction  by 2030) by facilitating the purchase or rental
of bicycles, including bicycle  repair and maintenance
costs into the "soft mobility pass", and by organising
campaigns  to promote  cycling,  including in urban areas;
•optimising motorised travel (target of 2,495 tCO₂e reduction
by 2030), mainly by organising car-free days and
implementing a car-sharing system between employees;
•supporting  the rollout of working from home (target of
1,182  tCO₂e  reduction by  2030).
La Banque Postale has  been managing arrangements for
business  travel since 2021 in  order to reduce the
associated carbon footprint, and opting for remote
meetings  wherever  possible. When business travel isnecessary, train travel (and more generally, the use of
public 
transport) should be used over air travel. For
commuting, 
La  Banque  Postale has been offering its
employees the "soft mobility pass" since 2023.  This is a
comprehensive offer that includes compensation of 50%
of 
the amount of the public transport subscription, the
sustainable mobility  package  of up to €220 per year and
the dissemination of useful information on commuting
and  employee safety.  In addition, La  Banque  Postale’s
home working agreement allows employees who are
eligible to benefit from 2  fixed  days of home  working  per
week in their roles, as well as a fixed rate of 10  annual
floating  days of  home working. This measure saved an
average of 6 tCO₂e per year according to the working
from home survey conducted in 2023.
Digital
Digital  efficiency  actions are  in place, in particular on the
responsible design of solutions, reducing the consumption
of IT  architecture and increasing the reuse of  equipment.
La Banque Postale aims to deploy a “responsible digital by
design” 
strategy, which incorporates ESG from the IT
consultation  and tendering phase.  Teams from the Bank
and  Network Information  Systems  Department (DSIBA)
work with the Purchasing Department to set ESG criteria.
An assessment grid of criteria is systematically included in
the specifications, and the main requirements are set out
in the contract.
Work 
is also being done on the responsible design of
digital solutions to ensure that they are always useful,
usable, used and  reusable.
In the use phase, targeted actions are carried out to reduce
the environmental footprint  of workstations (efficient
purchases and hardware settings), and on infrastructure
to manage consumption related to data centre  cooling.
Lastly, for end  of life, La Banque Postale is increasing the
reuse of its hardware (currently 30% of hardware is reused)
by making changes to the way in which asset managers
work, for example by discontinuing the destruction of
hard drives. In addition, awareness-raising among IT
sector  stakeholders and IT users is currently being rolled
out within La Banque  Postale ’s business  lines.
La  Banque  Postale  measures and  manages its  digital
footprint to guide the effectiveness of its actions. This
footprint 
includes the greenhouse gas emissions related
to its IT equipment, including computers, printing systems,
hubs, routers, switches and other network equipment,
telephony,  video projection equipment  and data centre
hardware, and building infrastructure such as air conditioning,
security and lighting.Please  see the glossary  on page 808 for definitions of the main CSR terms 2024 Universal  Registration Document     La Banque Postale 1292Sustainable performance
Environmental information
Other  levers  in the operational  scope
La Banque  Postale  has  launched a  responsible purchasing
approach,  consolidated and formalised as part of its RFAR
(Supplier 
Relations and Responsible Purchasing) certification,
which aims to  reduce the  negative impact of purchases
by La Banque Postale and its suppliers on the environment,
as 
well as encouraging positive impacts. La Banque Postale
is also  providing  more  detailed measurements of the
carbon  footprint of its suppliers, specifically targeting its
50 suppliers  with  the highest emissions.
The transition plan also includes additional actions for
better  management of the various components of the
operational  footprint.
The breakdown of the contributions of digital technology
and  responsible purchasing to  decarbonisation targets in
the operational scope has not yet been assessed. [E1_1_03]

The strategic and investment choices made today can
lock in the pathway of a company’s GHG emissions for
years to  come. The concept of locked-in emissions helps to
focus on this risk by identifying future GHG emissions
likely 
to be  caused  by the Company’s main assets, or by
products sold during the lifetime of these assets.
In seeking to apply this concept to its financial institution
activities, La Banque Postale reached the following conclusions:
Within 
the operational scope: the energy consumption of
IT servers and the depreciation of La  Banque  Postale’s
buildings 
generate future emissions associated with the
Company’s assets. However, in line with  the strategic
choices linked to locked-in emissions, as the operational
scope  constitutes less than 1% of La  Banque  Postale
Group’s 
carbon footprint, they are  not considered as a
transition 
risk by 2030-2050. They were therefore not
quantified at Group level.
CNP  Assurances has estimated locked-in emissions for its
scope  of approximately 2,691 tCO₂e per year related to the
consumption of IT servers and the depreciation of buildings.
Concerning 
the portfolios of financed activities,
La Banque Postale is not yet in a position to quantify the
locked-in emissions associated with its portfolios for two
main reasons:
•firstly,  the locked-in emissions should include the
locked-in  emissions  of portfolio companies. These are
not yet  available and will be published in the CSRD
publications of these  companies  from 2025;
•secondly, the life of an asset,  particularly in a portfolio of
loans, is uncertain, and this volatility does not allow
these  loans to  be considered as “locked-in”. Indeed, a
company 
or a retail customer can choose different
repayment terms  and can pay off a loan at any time.
While it is possible to estimate the evolution of the
portfolio 
with an average repayment term, it becomes
uncertain whether a specific loan term is associated
with an asset or company.  [E1_1_07]
La Banque Postale Group has not, moreover, invested any
significant  CapEx in connection with economic activities
related to coal, oil or gas.

is to build an adaptation plan to strengthen the Group’s
climate  resilience based on  its different geographical
locations  by integrating an in-depth understanding of its
vulnerability to climate hazards and all regional interactions.

particular  exposure to physical climate risk that could

concern the reduction  of the  exposure to  climate hazards
of investments in States, companies, buildings or forests,
as well  as the  integration of  climate  risks  into  its global
protection approach via the management of reinsurance
coverage  and a specific close monitoring of  changes in

Internal  carbon price
Since 2015, La  Banque  Postale has structured an internal
carbon  pricing  mechanism with  a dual  ambition:
•anticipate  changes in  the market price that could be
incorporated into climate risk  management;
•contribute to the achievement  of the Company’s
decarbonisation  targets.
New  work  on the  scope  will be carried out in  2025 in order
to comprehensively  cover  La Banque  Postale ’s operational
footprint.
The internal carbon pricing is organised around the Climate
and Biodiversity Impact Fund, a voluntary and  unprecedented
internal 
system for monetising La Banque Postale's carbon
footprint.
Drawing  inspiration from this system, CNP Assurances set
up the carbon and biodiversity fund mechanism based on
an internal carbon price for the first time in 2022.
The process  includes:
•an internal dimension enabling financing of renovation/
energy  optimisation work on buildings as well as an
internal 
call for  projects at all institutions. For these two
systems, 
monitoring indicators are managed in order to
estimate the  associated economic and environmental
gains . The return  on investment  of the projects  is also
analysed, which gives an annual view of the tonnes of
CO₂  equivalent avoided and the euros saved thanks to
the implementation of the  projects;
•an external dimension enabling the financing of carbon
sequestration  projects in France and abroad, as well as
biodiversity  conservation projects.  Here  too,  monitoring
indicators are managed to measure the tonnes of CO₂
equivalent sequestered per project, the species saved or
the square metres preserved. These various indicators
are monitored annually and presented to the Executive
Committee  to justify the  relevance of the system and its
contribution  to achieving  the reduction  targets.
For the  first  ten  editions,  a total  financial budget  of more
than €3 million  was used  to finance:
•internal  projects  to reduce greenhouse gas  emissions:
Since  the launch of the Climate and Biodiversity ImpactFund, 
La Banque Postale has financed 103 internal projects
aimed 
at reducing greenhouse gas emissions, thus avoiding
more than  7,529 tCO₂e. These  projects include energy
efficiency renovation, sustainable development
awareness  campaigns, creating fleets of electric bicycles
and scooters, the installation of solar water heaters and
solar panels, the greening of  roofs and the creation  of a
carpooling hub for employee commuting;
•external projects (national and international) to sequestrate
and  offset residual emissions as well as biodiversity
conservation 
projects. Partnerships  with players such as
CDC  Biodiversité and WWF were supported in order to
structure 
innovative approaches to the creation of
national carbon sinks.  [E1_8_01]
The internal carbon  price corresponds to a fictitious price
associated with one tCO₂e. [E1_8_02]
The internal carbon price applied  (€60) was decided by
La  Banque   Postale's Executive Committee based on the
assumptions and proposals  of the  Carbon  Disclosure
Project,  the Institut Montaigne report and the Blanchard-
Tirole  Commission, which recommend an average price of
around €65 per  tCO₂e in the European financial sector.
[E1_8_05]
The annual budget allocated to La Banque Postale’s Climate
and  Biodiversity Impact Fund and CNP  Assurances’
carbon  and biodiversity fund is calculated on the basis of
GHG emissions multiplied by the internal carbon price:

account 
are emissions for year N-2 (emissions under the

account 
are emissions for year N (Scopes 1 and 2 emissions,
representing 
1,495 tCO₂e and 276 tCO₂e, and indirect

2.1.11.1 GHG  emissions management  indicators
To manage its low-carbon pathway in its operational scope, La  Banque  Postale specifically monitors emissions related to
buildings, vehicles  and  digital  technology.
Emissions  related to the vehicle  fleet increased  by 14%
between 2023  and  2024. This  change is  due  to the  gradual
implementation of the vehicle policy, which is not yet in
full effect, as well as a better estimate in 2024 of the
vehicle  fleet  taken  into  account.
Between  2023 and 2024, greenhouse  gas (GHG) emissions
related to La   Banque  Postale’s IT infrastructure and data
centres 
decreased by 6%. This decrease is due to a number
of initiatives  implemented by La Banque  Postale Group:
•optimisation  of data centres: lockdown of cooling areas,
regulation of temperatures and optimised management
of volumes and  allocated spaces;
•extending  the  life of  equipment: reusing computer
equipment,  primarily through donations to social and
solidarity-based economy (SSE) players;•responsible  purchasing: using CSR  criteria for computer
equipment purchases, favouring EPEAT-certified equipment;
•awareness and training: training and awareness programmes
for employees on responsible digital  technology.
In addition, the transition from the “Green Argile” to the
“Aguaro” measurement tool in 2024 has enabled more
precise and detailed measurements to be taken, contributing
to better reliability and traceability of carbon footprint data.
As 
part of its status as a mission-led company,
La Banque Postale monitors low-carbon pathway indicators
which 
reflect SBTi commitments within its operating
scope. Crucially,  ensuring that its own operations comply
with these pathways  helps it to contribute  to combating
climate change, to strengthen its responsibility towards its
stakeholders  and to establish its  credibility as a mission-
led company.

2.2.2 Transition  plan
The consensus is confirmed on the need for financial
institutions 
to recognise the link between climate and nature,
taking into  account  the potential synergies and trade-offs
between these two topics. Transition plans must go beyond
simply 
incorporating nature into decarbonisation strategies,
and more specifically address the transformation of operations,
value chains  and  portfolios.  The  goal  is to align financial
flows with climate imperatives and to preserve biodiversity
based  on a more  holistic  approach.
Through  its financing  capacity, La Banque Postale plays a
role in supporting transformative  initiatives in economic
sectors with a strong impact on nature (such as agriculture,
chemicals and mining). To feed these sector-specific
transformation 
plans, La Banque Postale participates alongside
other  financial institutions in market initiatives such as
“Roquelaure  Entreprises et Biodiversité(1)", launched by the
French Ministry for the  Environmental Transition to
implement  the national biodiversity  strategy  (SNB).La Banque Postale carried out an initial scenario analysis
based  on the recommendations of the TNFD to identify
the biodiversity- and ecosystem-related risks and opportunities
for 2030 and 2050. The methodology used for this scenario
analysis is only qualitative, and differs from the climate
stress 
test. Indeed, to date, there is no agreed quantified
scenario concerning  the  evolution  of nature issues, and
the use  of qualitative scenarios is in  line  with  the TNFD
recommendations.
In its 2024 Climate and Nature report, La Banque Postale
describes  how it aims to further integrate nature  into its
risk management processes and decision-making. This first
report  focuses on the Corporate and  Investment Banking
activities of La  Banque  Postale SA, and is intended to be
extended to other La Banque Postale Group entities for its
future publications.
La  Banque  Postale aims to align its climate and nature
commitments to ensure consistency and compliance with
the targets set by the Bank in these two areas by adopting
a 
transition plan which encompasses these two subjects
no later than 2028. [E4_1_01] [E4_1_02] [E4_1_03] [E4_1_04] [E4_1_05]

throughout  its value chain to understand its relationship

following a scientific pathway to protect and restore

opportunities in  these  areas.
La Banque Postale is one of the  320 global organisations
(companies  and financial institutions) to have adopted
TNFD  at an early stage, in September 2023, to have
decided to anticipate  the changes caused by the erosion
of the state of nature  and to assess  how the Company
could be  impacted by these changes. In addition to the
impact analysis carried out as part of the CSRD,

La Banque  Postale carried out a more  in-depth  analysis of
its impacts, dependencies, risks and opportunities related
to nature on 39% of its financing portfolio (residential and
commercial  real  estate, commercial,  corporates  and
public sector and social economy), following the four steps
recommended 
by the TNFD LEAP  (Locate, Evaluate, Assess
and Prepare) approach. This analysis was carried out using
the Global Biodiversity  Score (GBS), a tool developed by
CDC  Biodiversité based on the use  of a wide  range of
input data, including economic  data, inventories and
physical  measurements.
A combined analysis was carried out between the results
of the "Locate" and "Evaluate" phases to assess the  extent
to which activities  financed by La  Banque  Postale could
have an impact  or a  strong dependency in particularly
sensitive  locations.  In addition, sector-specific  qualitative
grids have been developed to establish,  identify and
qualify the nature-related impacts  and dependencies for
La Banque Postale's priority sectors. This qualitative analysis
made it possible to specify  the results obtained during
the quantitative footprint measurement,  in particular on
the pressures or  scopes little covered by the footprint
measurement  tools. This task was carried out in five
sectors identified as priorities for La Banque Postale (real
estate,  food and beverage  manufacturing, transport and
warehousing,  energy production and distribution, the
health  and pharmaceutical sector). The combined analysis
of the impact, dependencies and locations of the financed
activities helps  to assess  the risks related  to nature.
Thus,  activities with particularly high impacts in sensitive
areas  may be  exposed to high transition risks. Likewise,
nature-based activities which are carried out in areas in
which nature  is damaged face  significant  physical  risks.
The assessment revealed that the impacts of the corporate
and public sector and social economy portfolios mainly
occur  in the  upstream value chain of the companies
financed, and are therefore linked to their purchases.
Terrestrial  impacts are mainly due to land use and climate
change, while  aquatic impacts  (freshwater)  are  due to
pollution  and wetland conversion. In addition, an in-depth
analysis was carried out to identify the main companies
contributing to  the  impact of  the  portfolio, to feed into a
reflection  within La  Banque  Postale on any engagement
policies  to be put in place.
Biodiversity  dependencies were also  assessed. Thus, 62%
of the Corporate portfolio technical reserves finance direct
activities  that are  critically dependent  on at least one
ecosystem  service (real estate, telecommunications and
construction  are  the  main critical  sectors). The most
widespread dependencies in  the  Corporate  and Public
sector  and social economy portfolios are water-related
ecosystem  services  (surface  water and  groundwater).
The  highest dependency is on  the ecosystem service for
soil stabilisation and erosion control. These analyses
confirm  the priorities  identified by La  Banque  Postale in
terms of the policies implemented.It is important to  specify  a few limits to the  measurement
of impacts and dependencies:
•retail banking direct reserves (excluding real estate),
equity 
securities and exposures to sovereigns (sovereign
bonds,  technical reserves at Banque de France  and
centralisation of passbook savings accounts) are currently
excluded, in the absence of a methodology and sufficient
data to  process them;
•the majority of the measurements were based on financial
data. 
It would benefit from improved accuracy, primarily
by including physical indicators specific to La Banque Postale’s
financing.  An initial reflection was carried out on the
physical  indicators to  be collected, and aims to have
indicators for each pressure exerted on biodiversity,
including climate change, in order to better manage
the associated  matters.

Actions of La Banque Postale Group subsidiaries
CNP Assurances includes biodiversity in the ESG filters of
listed 
equities and bonds. In addition to climate-related
matters, activities disrupting large or fragile areas, programmes
put 
in place to protect biodiversity and land use, controversies
over the use or management of natural resources, and
dependency on water and the treatment of discharges
into  water  are therefore  taken into account.
Real  estate has a significant impact on  biodiversity, both
during the construction  phase and the operating phase.
The CNP  Assurances SA "Green Works" charter imposes
rules on real estate  portfolio  management  companies  to
protect biodiversity, including respect for ecosystems during
the construction phase, choice of materials with a limited
impact 
on the environment and reducing waste and water
consumption. The Charter also provides for the study of
technical 
solutions favouring plants and technical solutions
that promote biodiversity, the circular  economy (reuse of
materials) and ecosystem services in buildings and green
spaces. 
CNP  Assurances also respects the principles of
sustainable 
management for the 54,986 hectares of forests
it owns, as defined by Société Forestière de la Caisse des Dépôts.Please  see the glossary  on page 808 for definitions of the main CSR terms 2024 Universal  Registration Document     La Banque Postale 1532Sustainable performance
Environmental information
Externally, 
CNP Assurances has integrated biodiversity into
its shareholder  engagement policy, and more specifically
in direct  dialogues  with the companies of which it  is a
shareholder: the target is to support CNP  Assurances’
strategy in favour of biodiversity. (including  through the
fight  against climate change), by encouraging companies
to make ambitious decisions to protect biodiversity, and
to publish information on the risks related to biodiversity
loss.  In 2024, CNP Assurances  discussed this subject with
five companies, i.e. in 31% of the direct conversations it held.
CNP   Assurances  measures the dependency  of portfolio
companies  on  ecosystem services  using the  BIA-GBS
methodology,  Biodiversity Impact Analytics powered  by
the Global Biodiversity Score. This work covers 98% of the
directly held  equity  and  bond  portfolio.
CNP   Assurances SA and its French subsidiaries are
participating  in the  “biodiversity marketplace  initiative”
launched in the spring of 2024, which brings together
11  institutional investors. Their target  is to promote the
development  of effective methodologies  for taking into
account biodiversity in financial management. The ambition
is to contribute to the achievement of international
target s for the protection and restoration of biodiversity,
and to advance  all institutional  investors in achieving their
investment  target s in favour  of nature and ecosystems.
In accordance with its biodiversity policy, LBP AM implements
a shareholder engagement action to help raise awareness
and  promote best  practices in terms of managing issues,
dependencies 
and impacts. It has led a number of collaborative
engagement campaigns on key topics such as sustainable
proteins, water management,  deforestation, the  use of
pesticides and pollution. LBP AM also monitors the biodiversity
footprint  of its portfolios.
LBP   AM relies on the ten people in its SRI Analysis and
Research  division, as well as  on various  specialised data
suppliers, who help  to conduct risk mapping and establish
priority actions. In  2023, LBP  AM developed a Biodiversity
rating  applicable  to companies in all sectors.
Since  2024, Louvre  Banque  Privée has measured its
biodiversity  footprint using the  BIA-GBS  database.
The  methodology is  being redesigned to be able to
integrate  UCITS.
The biodiversity footprint of the portfolio produced by BIA-
GBS  will enable  Louvre  Banque  Privée to:
•identify  the main pressures  on its portfolio;
•identify  the main contributors;
•on this basis, initiate a dialogue with these companies in
relation  to their  action plan to manage their impact
on biodiversity.Louvre Banque Privée has allocated resources to improving
this indicator management by subscribing to  dedicated
data subscriptions  and by increasing the  size  of its team of
ESG officers (currently five ESG officers in the discretionary
management team).
In 
addition, since 1 January 2023, Louvre Banque Privée requires
that all management mandates include biodiversity-related
issues in the  investment  policy.

In 2024, La Banque Postale Group, as a subsidiary, adopted
the Caisse des Dépôts Group’s water policy to address
the three  major  challenges  it faces:
•limited  and  scarce  water  resources;
•water  quality  and dedicated  infrastructure;
•flooding  and  soil sealing.
Firstly,  the aim is to support the water efficiency initiatives
of the  various  players  and play its part in the national
target of reducing  water consumption by 10% by 2030,
and secondly , to improve the  quality of bodies of water by
contributing in particular to the government target of
preserving 
100% of drinking water catchment areas by 2027
in order to achieve the targets of the Water Framework
Directive(1).
This Caisse des Dépôts policy is presented in three main parts:
•understand  the Group’s  impacts  and  risks;
•adopt  a water  saving approach;
•preserve  the quality of water and  infrastructure.
Each of these parts includes a series of commitments, targets
and  associated monitoring indicators. The first works  will
be carried  out in 2025.
The Group Risk Management Committee (GRMC) (of which
the Chairman of La Banque Postale's Executive  Board is a
member) is  responsible  for implementing  this policy.
[E3_MDR_P_01_06]

La Banque Postale first undertakes to identify its negative
impacts and the  dependency of its activities on water
resources  and natural freshwater ecosystems, in order to
manage  its related  water risks  and to preserve freshwater
and wetland ecosystems. It has made the following
commitments:
•by the  end  of 2025, produce  a water footprint or an
assessment  of the dependency of  water resources on
water-related ecosystem services;
•by the end of 2027, carry out an initial estimate of the
aquatic pollution (discharges) resulting from its operational
activities  or generated by  the invested or  financed
counterparties;
•by the end of 2027, assess exposure to the risk of drought
or water stress of the various financial portfolios (in French
and overseas French territories, and internationally where
relevant).Contribute to the water sobriety target
In order to participate in the national effort to reduce
water  consumption by 10% while meeting the challenges
related to the scarcity of water resources, La  Banque Postale
contributes to the target of water saving,  and offers
financing and  support to contribute to  modernising water
and sanitation networks. It supports stakeholders and
ensures the deployment of best practices in terms of water
consumption
. In addition, it is committed to deploying
financing tools dedicated to  the more efficient management
of water resources.
With 
respect to its commitments on financing portfolios,
La Banque Postale aims to:
•by the end of 2025, incorporate the general water saving
target 
into the ESG analysis criteria, and take into
account 
the degree of  water stress in  the area in which
the financing is located;
•for projects located in  areas of extremely high or high
water stress, take into account how aligned these projects
are 
with best  sectoral practices in terms of water
consumption, 
with the aim of not worsening the water
shortage situation in the  area concerned;
•deploy  financing tools dedicated to more efficient
management of  water resources. [E3_1_01] [E3_1_05] [E3_1_06]
Preserving the  quality  of water  and infrastructure
With the aim of preserving aquatic and wetland environments,
La  Banque  Postale is committed to reducing  its impact
on ecosystems that contribute to the water cycle, to
opting 
for nature-based solutions, and to contributing to
the rewilding and  restoration of these ecosystems. To do
so, La  Banque Postale has set itself  the following  targets:
•combat the  pollution  of aquatic environments;
•ensure the proper  functioning  of the  major water cycle;
•avoid  damaging  wetland areas.
At the same time, La  Banque  Postale has established
commitments for  the financing portfolios:
•exclude any financing or investment in companies in
which 
more than 20% of revenue comes from the
manufacture or sale of pesticides;
•deploy  tools to improve the quality of water resources
via loans to public sanitation services or water agencies.

developed  by La  Banque  Postale in partnership  with

(for more information on the IWF, see  focus point:
The Impact Weighting  Factor (IWF)) .
Since  2019, the SFIL/La  Banque  Postale financing system
for local  authorities and  their groups  has offered a "green
loan" topical offer. The "Sustainable management of water
and sanitation' component" is partly dedicated to managing
the small water  cycle, by financing investments  made by
public drinking  water and sanitation  services.
La Banque Postale also offers a bridging loan to pre-finance
subsidies  to water  agencies with  the aim of securing
supplies,  reducing leaks in networks, reuse of treated
wastewater,  etc.
In addition, La  Banque Postale , as part  of its Climate and
Biodiversity Impact Fund, finances projects to reduce water
consumption
.
Actio ns are also taken  by La  Banque  Postale ’s subsidiaries:
•CNP Assurances’ “Green Works” Charter requires companies
managing  directly owned real estate portfolios to limit
water  consumption and supply water that meets quality
requirements ;
•LBP  AM  is a member of  the  Valuing  Water initiative, led
by the NGO CERES, which raises awareness on the
protection of water  resources;
•Louvre   Banque  Privée is stepping up the quantitative
monitoring  of PAIs (adverse impacts  under the SFDR), in
particular  “emissions to water”. [E3_MDR_A_01_12]
Following the exercise to measure the impacts, dependencies,
risks and opportunities on its balance sheet and off-balance
sheet  exposures conducted in 2023-2024, discussions will
be undertaken to gradually complete the impact reduction
actions.  [E3_MDR_A_13_14]
Target  areas  exposed to water  risks
As part of  the 2023 Climate and Nature report,
La Banque  Postale carried out  an analysis of the location
of financing  in 2024.This analysis identified the activities financed by
La  Banque  Postale which are located in sensitive areas,
implying 
a specific risk for the activities present in these
areas. These  areas were identified according to several
criteria, including the level  of water stress.
The results show that the risk levels with at least two high-
risk 
criteria cover nearly 65% of the areas financed. These areas
are located in areas that are important for biodiversity,
have high ecological integrity or are subject to water stress.
The analysis highlights two types of priority locations for
La Banque Postale:
•those concentrating a significant portion of potential
building 
land in areas with average overall risk, such as
Île-de-France;
•those 
particularly important for nature, even if the financed
surface area is smaller, particularly in certain locations in
the South-East of France, where the overall risk is very high.
This 
first assessment will  then make it possible to establish
concrete  actions to  limit the  impacts of the activities
financed in  water-risk  areas.
By the  end of 2027, CNP  Assurances will map the assets
of its various financial portfolios located in areas with high
and  extremely high water stress  risk (in France and
internationally). 
By the end of 2026, CNP  Assurances will
also 
map its sites and real estate assets in water-stressed
areas 
(in France and internationally). This work will be
carried out within the limits of the available tools and data.
Finally, LBP AM is raising awareness among the companies
in which it invests  to map out water abstraction sites and
identify areas with high water stress, and to implement a
study 
of the impact of abstraction on  local populations.
The actions take the form of ad hoc commitments  with
the companies  most exposed to the risk. [E3_2_03]

Green  Asset  Ratio  (GAR) calculation  principles
The GAR is the ratio of Green  Taxonomy-aligned assets to total assets, and is the Taxonomy’s  key performance indicator.
It identifies  the proportion of the Bank’s total assets  invested  in sustainable  economic  activities.
* Non-Financial Reporting  Directive
Based  on total assets, the assets included in the GAR’s
numerator  are identified by applying the Green Taxonomy
technical  screening criteria to selected types of products
and  counterparties.
a) The  assets covered  by the analysis correspond to total
on-balance sheet assets minus sovereign, central bank
and  supranational exposures and the trading book.
These covered assets represent the GAR’s denominator.
b) Some  assets, such as exposures to companies not subject
to the Non-Financial Reporting Directive (NFRD) and
interbank 
loans, are only excluded from the numerator,
such that only certain exposures are analysed for Taxonomy
eligibility. 
Due to this difference in scope between the
GAR numerator and denominator, a bank’s Taxonomy-
eligible asset ratio and alignment ratio will always be less
than 100%. This is because the exposures concerned bythe 
exclusion rules will not be subjected to any alignment
analysis 
separately from the analysis of the assets’
environmental 
characteristics. For example, a loan to an
SME for the construction of a wind  farm could not be
included in the GAR’s numerator.
c)An activity qualifies for inclusion in the alignment analysis
provided 
that the technical criteria are specified in the
regulation. Certain activities, such as farming, do not qualify
as Taxonomy-eligible at this stage.
d)Among the Taxonomy-eligible assets, specialised financing
that meets the Taxonomy criteria is considered as aligned.
Loans 
qualified as general purpose financing are included
based on  the alignment ratios published by the
counterparties. An asset may only be considered as
aligned with a single environmental target to avoid it
being counted twice.

The policies presented below respond directly  to positive
impacts concerning favourable working conditions for the
Group’s 
own workforce, negative impacts concerning working
conditions  that harm the physical or mental health of
employees, and risks related to  the quality of life at work
and working  conditions of  employees.
The Quality of Work Life and Working Conditions (QWLWC)
policy has been implemented by the Human Resources
Department for the companies of La  Banque  Postale's
Economic  and Social Unit (UES), and meets the following
targets:
•Define  and implement a global QWLWC approach for
all stakeholders in the Company, based on the following
topics:
•Work 
content: streamlining the organisation and working
methods in order to promote workload regulation;
•Prevention and health at work: protecting the physical
and mental  health of employees;
•Work  relations : facilitating work-life balance;
•tackling information overload (infobesity);
•Create  a multi-disciplinary approach to the primary
prevention  of occupational risks, in order to protect the
physical and mental health and safety of employees
and,  more generally, contribute to their well-being at
work,  broken  down  into  various phases:
•Analyse  and objectify situations  by relying specifically
on indicators;
•Build the approach by involving the various stakeholders;
•Involve  all stakeholders in the Company in QWLWC
issues;
•Use trial and error as part of a continuous improvement
approach;
•Monitor the actions implemented  and  progress made;
•Promote  good work relationships at every stage of
employees’  professional lives by  making integration a
driver of alignment with the Company's values and culture
and by ensuring a work-life balance throughout their career.
These provisions are in line with the legal and regulatory
framework  laid down  in particular by the  French Labour
Code, as well as by any regulations applicable in the business
segment, via the  French National Collective  Agreement
on Banking for La  Banque  Postale and other branch
agreements  for the  business  segments of each entity.
After  in-depth  negotiations,  the QWLWC agreement  was
signed on 11 September 2023 by three representative trade
unions. The provisions are published on the intranet, and
are accessible to  all employees.  An annual commission
monitors  the QWLWC agreement. This enables both the
stakeholders who have contributed to its drafting and are
responsible for its implementation, and the social partners,
to monitor  the proper implementation of the agreement.
In addition, CNP  Assurances has a QWLWC agreement
that  addresses  the level of  employee  engagement  and
well-being.  It is therefore committed to structuring and
organising 
diversity and inclusion initiatives and stakeholders
by setting up  diversity and inclusion governance at the
international  level, including for its subsidiaries. [S1_1_01]

The policies presented in this paragraph respond to the
positive 
and negative impacts and risks related to diversity

Policies applicable  to diversity  and inclusion
The Diversity  and Inclusion policy is redefined every three
years 
in the related social agreement. It is implemented by
the Human Resources Department and applies to the
entire scope and to employees of La  Banque Postale UES.
The Diversity and Inclusion policy is based  on the  five
pillars of  Diversity:
•Disability: recruitment of people with RQTH (disabled
worker) 
status with equal skills, and obtaining recognition
of disabled  worker status  for our current employees;
•Generations: keeping older people in employment, bringing
young people into the job market, intergenerational diversity;
•Parity: 
gender equality, gender balance, combating everyday
sexism,  equal  treatment, parity of governing bodies;
•LGBT+: develop a respectful and inclusive working
environment for  LGBT+ people, with specific actions to
improve their well-being and inclusion;
•Social/Ethnic  origins: creating an inclusive collective
experience to ensure fairness at all stages of employee
life with the Company.
The diversity policy is built with experts, charities, the Human
Resources 
Department and employees. It is distributed
internally (on the intranet) and externally (on the website).
[S1_1_10]
La  Banque   Postale UES’ Diversity and Inclusion policy
covers all the grounds for discrimination identified by law
(26 listed by the legislator to date), including sex, gender,

systematic recruitment  of RQTH (Recognition of the status

parity  indicator;

To implement all of these commitments, every year,
La  Banque  Postale Group  proposes a comprehensive
action  plan to combat all forms of  discrimination andstrengthen the inclusion of  all people likely to be discriminated

more  generally all  forms of inhuman, cruel or degrading
treatment;
•prohibiting

3.1.4 Reporting and  remediation process
Reporting  distressing  situations  at work
For La Banque  Postale UES,  the procedure  set up by the
system for dealing with distressing situations at work is
conducted 
in compliance with the  principle of the presumption
of innocence, with complete impartiality and with the discretion
necessary to protect each person's dignity and privacy.
No information is disclosed beyond the circle of stakeholders.
Any employee who considers  themself to be a victim of
harassment  at work, or who is in a distressing  situation
that could harm their physical or mental health, has the
option 
of reporting this to their manager, the occupational
health 
service, employee representatives, harassment officers
or the ethics officer  (via the whistleblowing system  or the
social assistance  service).
Distressing situations at work that may be reported include
moral  harassment, sexual harassment,  sexist behaviour,
but also  any  problem  that  causes  a situation of  unease, or
even professional  burnout.
Employees  have several specific channels to raise their
concerns.  The Company has set up these channels, which
are partially implemented by experts (S EC, contact with
employee representatives, whistleblowing system,  system
for dealing with distressing situations at work).
​Reports  from employees can be received by the manager,
the various HR stakeholders (human resources manager,
occupational health department), employee representatives,
harassment  officers, the social worker or by the ethics
officer  (directly  or via the  whistleblowing platform). [S1_3_02]
La  Banque  Postale UES ensures that its employees are
informed  of the existence of this whistleblowing system
and  how it is used, via the Group's intranet. As part of the
recruitment process, all new Group employees receive a
paperless 
copy  of the  Internal Rules, to which  the  code of
conduct is attached. The latter contains detailed information
on the whistleblowing  channels  available to them.
All information concerning whistleblowing channels is also
available on the intranet site. In addition to this information,
the intranet also provides details of other mechanisms
such 
as the contacts of employee representatives and ways
of reporting distressing situations at work. To increase
awareness and  ensure that  employees  can have full
confidence in these mechanisms, training and communication
actions are regularly organised. Since 2024, a  tool called
Confirmodoc has been set up to verify the distribution of
the code of c onduct  to all employees and third parties
acting  for the Group.  [S1_3_06]  [S1_3_08]Processing reports
Reports are processed as quickly as possible by the Group’s
Human Resources Department, and recorded  in a dedicated
register.
Upon 
receipt of the report, the Human Resources Department
sets 
up a listening phase within 15 days. The purpose of
this first phase is to identify,  analyse and guide the alert in
order to verify whether the system is adapted to the
situation  of the employee  concerned.
The precautionary principle requires Human  Resources
managers in charge  of listening to  assess:
•whether the distressing situation of the person(s) requires
a referral to occupational health;
•whether 
there is a need for any temporary measures to
ensure the protection and safety of the employees involved.
At the  end  of the listening phase:
•if the information gathered at this stage allows the Human
Resources 
Department to make a decision, the investigation
phase as detailed below is not opened;
•if the information gathered at this stage does not allow
the Human Resources Department to make a decision,
the investigation phase is  opened.
During the investigation phase, a joint steering committee
is set up,  composed of two  representatives of the Human
Resources 
Department, the secretary of the Social and
Economic 
Committee (SEC) and the rapporteur of the
Health, Safety and Working Conditions Commission of the
SEC. This phase allows the two specialised HR contacts to
investigate 
any witnesses or persons who can  shed light
on the  situation, in  order  to identify  the  actions to be
taken to remedy it.
In the interests of combating moral harassment,  sexual
harassment and sexist behaviour, the  SEC and Human
Resources Department contacts are  responsible for
guiding, informing and supporting the employees who
contact them. Employees are informed of the regulations
in 
force through information, prevention and awareness-
raising actions.
At the end of any investigation phase, the Human Resources
Department 
decides on the actions to be implemented.
For example, these may include support measures provided
by the Company and intended to provide  medical and
psychological support  to the  victim.
The Human Resources  Department may  implement a
number of corrective measures:
•Disciplinary measures: employees are required to comply
with 
the internal rules and the code of conduct, which
specify the sanctions incurred in the event of moral or
sexual 
harassment, and sexist or violent acts. These sanctions
may  go as far as  dismissal for  gross  misconduct;
•Measures on work organisation and processes: if the
investigation 
reveals problems inherent in the work
organisation 
and processes implemented within the
team,  the Human Resources Department shall work
with 
the relevant department to take any measures that
it 
deems fit to resolve  the issue.  The effectiveness  of the
implemented  measures is monitored by the Human
Resources Department. 
[S1_3_05] [S1_4_02]Please  see the glossary  on page 808 for definitions of the main CSR terms 2024 Universal  Registration Document     La Banque Postale 1752Sustainable performance
Social information
The Employee Relations Department, which is affiliated to
the 
Human Resources Department, represents the Company
and  brings its policy before the employee representative
bodies (Social and  Economic  Committee,  employee
representatives as a whole), and ensures the monitoring
and  coordination  of these  channels.
The system for dealing with  distressing situations at work
is monitored by the Human Resources Department, which
records reports and ensures that the system is effectively
deployed and that individual situations are dealt with. [S1_3_07]
Process  for distressing situations at work 
in the subsidiaries
In its agreements, CNP Assurances describes its commitments
to remedy the negative impacts on its employees, and
exercises  constant due diligence to prevent any risk of
discrimination.
It has various specific reporting channels to collect and
process 
any report or alert submitted by a CNP Assurances
Group employee:
•Integrity  Line  whistleblowing system (online intranet
platform): reports are collected and processed by the

•Internal 
Social Mediation (by email or telephone): reports
are processed  by the Mediator via an encrypted file.
CNP   Assurances ensures that its employees have access
to whistleblowing  and  report  processing  systems.
In addition, throughout the Group  reports can  be made
through line managers or human resources teams. The Group
whistleblowing system is also available to all employees of
the subsidiaries.  [S1_3_01]
Whistleblowing  system
A system for collecting and processing ethics reports is also
available  to all La  Banque Postale Group employees via a
specific platform. This system is described in Section 2.4.1.3.5
“Independence and accessibility of the whistleblowing system”.
Information 
on the system is provided to employees, notably
through the code  of conduct.  [S1_3_05]  [S1_4_02]
Whistleblower protection is also in place, in accordance
with  the rules.  [S1_3_09]
The whistleblowing system is monitored by the Compliance
Department through the Ethics teams. A report on the

(anonymised)  is presented  to the Supervisory Board on an

3.1.5.1 Actions implemented

Avoidance of  negative impacts
La  Banque  Postale Group implements various actions to
prevent  or mitigate its potential negative impacts on its
employees.
Working 
conditions affecting the physical or mental health
of employees (
e.g. stress, burnout, musculoskeletal disorders)
To remedy the impacts related to working conditions, an
employment 
law division supports local HR players to take
charge of all collective or individual files  on all aspects of
employee relations. The Life at Work division works in
conjunction 
with the health service to identify and implement
solutions adap ted to the observed impacts.
The specific actions carried out in 2024 to avoid the negative
impacts of working  conditions include:
•Preventing traffic accidents;
•Preventing visual and  hearing  fatigue;
•Preventing a sedentary lifestyle.
Workstation  adjustments were also made to prevent or
mitigate  musculoskeletal disorders.
The use of work  tools  and  preventing  information
overload  are also concerns for La Banque Postale UES. In
this respect, the practices for using work tools and the
information  overload prevention system are available on
the intranet.
These issues are particularly topical due to the increased
popularity  of hybrid working methods, and particularly
working from home.
Work and meeting organisation practices,  particularly in
hybrid mode, are also reiterated in the new home-working
agreement (renewed  for three years  in 2024). They will be
specifically supported by managers in 2025.
As part of the roll-out of the new home-working agreement,
an

respective countries.  [S1_12_03]

3.1.7.9 Remuneration gap
In 2024, the overall remuneration gap between women
and men was 16.7%. The remuneration gap between
women and men is mainly related to the job structure:
women  are more represented than men at lower grade
levels,  while  this trend is  reversed  at higher levels.
Motivated by the “Diversity and professional equality”
agreement  of 2024, La Banque  Postale has implemented
substantial actions to remedy this, such as ensuring gender
diversity in  the  business lines  (under-represented gender
recruitment  with  equal skills, developing  partnerships
with schools and  charities to develop the attractiveness of
so-called "gendered" professions, and boosting the careers
of women through  community events (Girlz in the Bank,
etc.) as well  as preventing  everyday  sexism.
In addition to these actions, La  Banque   Postale allocates
an overall budget of €600,000  per year to reducing
unjustified  remuneration  gaps.
The ratio between the highest salary and  the median
salary is 10.4, reflecting a moderation of the remuneration gap
within  the  Group,  in line  with the values  of inclusion  and
social responsibility that drive us.Calculation methodology and background information
The gender remuneration  gap compares the  gross hourly
remuneration paid to women during the financial year to
that 
paid to  men. Th is hourly remuneration includes, on
an annual basis, fixed remuneration, bonuses and benefits
paid, annual and long-term variable remuneration paid,
excluding profit-sharing and matching contributions.
The ratio between the highest remuneration and the median
remuneration compares the total annual remuneration
(remuneration components mentioned above, also including
profit-sharing bonuses paid as well as  any matching
contributions) of the person receiving the highest remuneration
to the total annual median remuneration of all other
employees. 
The employees taken into account are those
with permanent or temporary employment  contracts,
working with La  Banque  Postale Group for at least three
months of the financial year.
Work-study students were excluded from these calculations
given that the work-study (“alternant”)  status is  specific to
France, and that work-study contracts are governed by a
statutory  remuneration grid and are not subject to a
discretionary wage. As a result, including work-study students
would mean that  the analysis  could not be refined.
These indicators are calculated by aggregating the indicators
of CNP Assurances and those of the rest of La Banque Postale
Group, in proportion to th e workforce of each scope.
The number of La Financière de l’Échiquier employees outside
France 
(10) could not be included in the calculations for

Scope
Workers in the  upstream value chain are key stakeholders
for La  Banque  Postale.  This  entire population is likely  to be
impacted by the Group. Two main types of workers are
concerned:
•Employees  working on one of La Banque Postale’s sites
(head office, subsidiaries, post offices) but who are not
part of the workforce;
•Workers working  for La Banque  Postale ’s suppliers.
The workers integrated into the Company's downstream
value  chain (workers of the financed companies) are dealt
with in Section 2.3.2.3 “Workers in the downstream value chain”.
Service 
providers in the building, maintenance and logistics
sectors  are more exposed  to the potential  impacts of any
failure  of safety  rules. In addition, workers belonging to
vulnerable groups (older employees, people with disabilities,
ethnic minorities) are more exposed to the potential impacts
of discrimination  and inequality.  [S2_SBM_3_01] [S2_SBM_3_02]
[S2_SBM_3_03]
In order to identify these specific groups, an ESG risk  rating
is carried out to assess third-party suppliers. It incorporates
the specific working conditions applicable to the different
types  of workers within the value chain, for example  by
differentiating between consulting services where risks
are 
mainly related to mental load, and maintenance activities,
which are more exposed to physical risks or precarious
working  conditions.  This  differentiation makes  it possible
to identify particularly exposed groups more precisely and
to adapt  prevention and  due  diligence  measures
accordingly.  [S2_SBM_3_08]La  Banque  Postale recognises that social factors in the
value 
chain do not affect all workers in the same way.
These 
risks may vary depending on the geographical
location 
of the suppliers (for CNP Assurances in particular),
the 
business segment and the contract type. For example,
workers 
operating in sensitive regions may face social or
safety 
risks at work. To mitigate these risks, La Banque Postale
adopts specific clauses in contracts, targeted audits and
implements a whistleblowing  system.  [S2_SBM_3_09]
Identified impacts, risks and opportunities
The identified material impacts on workers in the upstream
value chain  are as follows:
•Actual positive impacts by  contributing to improving
working conditions, and the protection and inclusion of
workers 
in the value chain of own operations and
service activities;
•Potential negative impacts in the  event of poor working
conditions 
(unequal  remuneration, safety,  etc.),  forced
labour or child labour within companies in the value chain
of own operations (suppliers, etc.) and service activities.
La  Banque  Postale ’s responsible purchasing strategy
generates positive impacts on workers in the value chain,
as it helps to improve the working conditions of employees
in 
its value chain. In 2022, La  Banque  Postale became  a
mission-led company, making its community foundations
the key  driver of  its performance in support of the  just
transition.  In this context, its business  model directly
interacts with six Sustainable Development  Goals (SDGs),
and  it publishes monitoring indicators in relation to these
Goals. 
The purchasing strategy, which takes into account
the identified impacts on workers in the value chain,
contributes to  the achievement of these SDGs.

These positive impacts cover all  workers in the value chain

The requirement  to comply with the principles of the  UN
Global Compact and the fundamental conventions of the
International
 Labour Organization (ILO), as well as the

providers and suppliers, contribute to the improvement of
working  conditions. They promote a healthy, safe and
inclusive  work  environment. [S2_SBM_3_06]
The potential negative impacts identified on workers in
the value chain are the result of the  business model.
La  Banque  Postale is a tertiary sector company that
outsources 
or subcontracts a significant  portion of its own
operations.  Being positioned in France and operating its
activities mainly in France (excluding CNP  Assurances),
La Banque Postale mainly relies on French and European
suppliers for the outsourcing of its services and subcontracting.
In this context, the activity of  its leading subcontractors is
carried out in compliance with European labour law and
the 
standards of the United Nations Global Compact, thereby
limiting  the potential of the  negative  impacts  identified.
The management and monitoring  of the Responsible
Purchasing  Charter targets guide La  Banque  Postale’s
purchasing  strategy. For example, the environmental and
social  commitments made as part of La Banque Postale’s
mission-led company and strategic plan for 2030 led it to
approve  La Poste  Group’s Purchasing policy and to draft
its 
“Responsible Purchasing Approach”, as well as confirming
its 
commitment to the “Supplier Relations and Responsible
Purchasing (RFAR)” approach. This resulted in the signing
of the RFAR charter in September 2022, while the
La  Banque  Postale SA and CNP   Assurances entities
obtained the RFAR certification  in September 2023.
The RFAR certification process  for banking subsidiaries of
La Banque  Postale SA  will be launched from 2025.
The potential negative impacts identified are related to
the following  events:
•Poor  application of security  measures;
•Unequal  remuneration  (women/men, executive salaries)
due to  inadequate  remuneration policies  among
subcontractors;
•Acts of discrimination;
•Forced  labour  or child labour. [S2_SBM_3_05]
No material opportunities arising from the impacts on
workers  in the value  chain were  identified.
However,  two material  risks  stand  out:
•Risk  of financial  loss due to failures  in assessing
La Banque Postale’s partners (service providers, suppliers
or 
distributors) in an environment shaped by the transition
towards  a more equitable  and  inclusive society (with
more or less rapid regulatory changes in the face of social
injustice, changes in consumer behaviour and markets, etc.);
•Termination  or temporary decrease in the activity of a
major  service  provider,  supplier  or distributor resulting
in financial  losses.These risks are taken into account in La Poste Group’s
Purchasing Charter, one of the  main areas of which is  to
limit dependency on suppliers. This Charter applies to all
subsidiaries 
majority owned by La  Banque  Postale.
These  risks are therefore considered within the scope of
own 
operations for a majority of the  Group’s entities.
In 
addition, the ESG risks associated with products and
services are included in the Group’s overall risk mapping,
which feeds into its strategy.
These risks are gross risks, which can arise in the event of
poorly  managed dependency on suppliers. [S2_SBM_3_07]
Risks  of forced  labou r and child labour
La  Banque  Postale and most of its subsidiaries operate
mainly  in the tertiary sector in France,  a country in which
the risks of  forced labour,  compulsory labour  and child
labour are generally considered low.
CNP  Assurances operates in the tertiary sector in France,
Europe 
and Latin America. Although CNP Assurances’ activities
are 
concentrated in regions in which the risks of forced
labour and child labour are  low, the  Company remains
vigilant on these issues, in accordance with regulations
and international  initiatives in  force.  [S2_SBM_3_04]

3.2.2.2 Applicable policies
La  Banque  Postale Group is actively committed to the
workers in its upstream value chain, in order to  limit the
negative impacts and develop the positive impacts that it
may  have on this group of people. These commitments
include various  policies.
The Responsible and Ethical Purchasing Charter formalises
the commitments of La  Banque  Postale Group to its
customers,  employees, society, the regions and the planet,
with the aim of  it being  jointly imple mented by its
employees, suppliers  and  subcontractors. This charter
requires La  Banque  Postale Group’s service providers to
comply  with a certain number of principles, and to ensure
that the same applies to their  subcontractors.
The following commitments are defined by  the Charter
and enable La Banque Postale to contribute to establishing
good working conditions and respect for fundamental rights
throughout the value chain. Suppliers therefore undertake to:
•develop 
management and working conditions that respect
human dignity and the rights of workers, and in particular
comply with  the  National Interprofessional Agreement
of 2 July 2008 on stress  at work, in order to prevent
psychosocial risks;
•refrain from any  form  of work  that, due to the  conditions
in which it is carried out, may  be detrimental  to health
or safety;
•comply with legislation on the management of working
hours, remuneration, training and trade union rights;
•respect 
the principles of the Global Compact, the eight
fundamental 
conventions of the ILO (International Labour
Organization) and the ILO  Declaration on Fundamental
Principles  and Rights  at Work, aimed in particular at
combating forced labour, child labour and discrimination;
•implement 
all means necessary to comply with the
principles set  out by the Charter throughout their design,
supply and manufacturing chain of the  products or
services they offer to La   Banque  Postale,  including in
non-signatory countries of ILO conventions in which

Social information
La Banque Postale Group’s Responsible Purchasing Charter is
appended to and systematically included in the product
and  service  contracts  signed between La Banque  Postale
and  its suppliers, and is accessible via a link in the General
Purchasing Conditions shown on the back of purchase orders.
The Responsible Purchasing  Charter  was  approved
by  La  Banque  Postale  Group’s Executive Committee.
Its implementation and monitoring are the responsibility
of the Purchasing  Department.
For several years, La Poste Group has forged close relationships
with stakeholders on the subject of responsible purchasing.
In particular, it is an active member of the Observatoire
des Achats Responsables (ObsAR). As a subsidiary of
La  Poste Group, La  Banque  Postale’s Responsible and
Ethical Purchasing Charter is a continuation of this approach.
La Poste Group’s Responsible Purchasing policy has been
adopted  as a reference document  by La  Banque  Postale.
It is based  on four pillars:
•Pillar  1: Enforce  and  promote  human rights throughout
supply chains;
•Pillar  2: Reduce  the negative impact of  purchases and
suppliers on the environment and encourage positive
impacts;
•Pillar 
3: Promote social inclusion and contribute, through
purchases, 
to the development of the regional economic
and social  fabric;
•Pillar 4: Consolidate responsible and ethical relationships
with  suppliers.
To promote inclusion through its purchases, La Poste Group
is looking for suppliers committed to the integration of
people 
who are isolated from employment and contributing
to the development of the regions in which they operate,
particularly  in vulnerable regions. The Group is committed
to facilitating access to its markets for the structures
involved,  and encourages its suppliers to have a positive
impact in terms of inclusion in their region, through their
subcontracting  chain.
La Poste Group ’s Responsible Purchasing policy is approved
by the Group’s Executive Committee. Its implementation
and  monitoring are the responsibility of the Group’s
Purchasing  Department. Within La  Banque  Postale , the
Purchasing  Department  is responsible  for implementing
this policy  and  ensuring that it is  operational.
According to the international standard ISO 204001, La Poste
Group  defines responsible  purchasing as  “a purchase with
the most positive environmental, social and economic
impacts  possible  over  the entire life cycle”.
The principles of this policy are reiterated and supplemented
in La  Banque   Postale Group’s body of documents and
contractual agreements with each stakeholder. In addition,
La Poste Group’s Responsible Purchasing policy is available
on its website.
La Poste Group ’s Respo nsible  Purchasing policy  and
La  Banque   Postale Group’s Responsible and Ethical
Purchasing  Charter apply to the entire value chain and to
all of La  Banque  Postale Group’s purchasing activities,
whether  in France or internationally.The supplier assessment procedure is intended to determine
the rules to be followed in order to  assess  the risks
associated with La Banque Postale Group’s suppliers, and
to decide on any action to be taken, whether before
entering 
into a contractual relationship or during the
performance  of the contract.  The Group’s suppliers  must
be assessed to cover the risks that the relationship with
them may bring  in terms of:
•Financial  risks;
•Risks of  corruption (French  Sapin II law);
•Documentary risk (French  Due  diligence  law);
•ESG risks  (French Due diligence law).
Criteria such as the supplier’s financial health, dependency
rate, 
environmental compliance and Human Rights risks
are assessed.
In addition, the Purchasing Manual is a document for use
by the Purchasing  Department which will be rolled out
within the Group’s Purchasing teams from 2025. It presents
the organisation and  describes the macro-processes to
be applied by Purchasing staff for La  Banque  Postale
Group purchases. In particular, it specifies the structure of
the tender assessment grid. This multi-criteria assessment
approach  manages the risk of financial loss related to a
failure 
in the  assessment of suppliers, service providers or
distributors, in a context of transition to a more equitable
and inclusive society.
All of the  documents applicable by La   Banque  Postale
Group’s Purchasing function can be consulted by all
employees of the Purchasing Department on the private
intranet. 
The purchasing procedure, operating methods
and models required by specifiers to apply the purchasing
process are available on the public intranet.  [S2_MDR_P_01_06]

3.2.3.5 Action plans  and  resources
Measures and actions  implemented
La  Banque  Postale Group as a whole implements
ambitious 
and consistent policies to prevent, mitigate and
remedy  negative impacts on human rights, based on
approaches  adapted to its various entities. These efforts,
although  complementary, are adapted  to the specificities
of the activities of each  of the subsidiaries.
For the entire La Banque Postale Group, a key cross-functional
initiative 
is employee awareness-raising. In order to minimise
and prevent the negative impacts  of degraded working
conditions, forced labour or child  labour in the portfolio
companies, 
La  Banque  Postale has designed and rolled
out in 2024  an e-learning training module dedicated to
human rights. This training, accessible to all employees,
aims to strengthen their  knowledge of fundamental
human rights and specific issues such as  how to combat
forced  labour  and  child labour.
La Banque Postale’s  subsidiaries have put in place a framework
that promotes the prevention of negative impacts  on the
human rights of workers in  the downstream  value chain,
which is adapted  to their activity.
CNP  Assurances
With  regard to the shares and bonds held directly by
CNP Assurances SA and its French subsidiaries, the selection
of assets takes  human rights matters into account by
looking  at the  ESG ratings  of companies.  The  ESG  rating of
companies and issuers is based on the GREaT methodology
developed 
by LBP AM. This approach also looks at sustainable
management of resources. Two  social criteria are prioritised:
•Working conditions: ensuring that employees, subcontractors
and  suppliers  work in good  health and safety conditions;
•Human  rights: ensuring that  trade union freedoms and
the fundamental human rights of employees, subcontractors
and suppliers  are respected.
LBP  AM
As a subsidiary  specialising in asset management, LBP AM
translates 
these commitments through targeted practices
and robust  methodologies.
LBP  AM’s Human Rights policy is in line with international
standards  and  European regulatory  requirements, such as
the SFDR,  and  is based  on several areas:
•integration  of human rights in asset management: risks
relating  to value  chain workers are integrated  into the
analysis, selection and  monitoring  of assets  using  SRI
rating  tools. These tools assess issuers on their ability to
prevent, mitigate and remedy severe human rights impacts.
•sustainability  analysis  methodology:  LBP   AM  applies a
methodology  that  systematically verifies that  issuers
respect human rights and are not associated with serious
controversies. This methodology is  aligned with the
minimum sustainable investment thresholds for products
classified in Article 8  and  Article  9 of the SFDR.•exclusion policy: LBP AM excludes companies associated
with serious violations of  fundamental ethical standards,
with 
an extended application to its open-ended funds
and, according to investors, to dedicated funds or mandates.
•shareholder 
engagement: LBP AM actively communicates
with 
invested companies to encourage them to strengthen
their human rights due diligence practices, in accordance
with the principles of the United Nations Global Compact,
the UNGP and the  OECD  Guidelines.
Louvre  Banque  Privée
For its part,  Louvre Banque  Privée adapts these commitments
to the specific nature of its activities, primarily by integrating
a 
strengthened qualitative analysis within its  operational
framework. Louvre  Banque  Privée relies on a framework
designed to manage the material  impacts, risks and
opportunities 
related to workers in the value chain.
This framework is based on:
•the use of ESG  data providers to identify serious controversies
and  human rights  violations.
•a team of  internal ESG contacts (for qualitative analysis).
[S2_MDR_A_01_12] [S2_4_01]
Monitoring  the effectiveness of actions
The 
exclusion and engagement actions provided for by
the LBP AM's Human Rights policy are primarily implemented
through two SRI  Committees:
•The 
GREaT Committee, which steers the cross-functional
deployment of engagement and exclusion policies and
decides on the implementation of the various components
of the  exclusion policy, in particular  decision-making
relating  to the LBP  AM’s Standards policy.  The GREaT
Committee monitors issuers on the standards and
exclusion watchlist and  may, in the event of positive or
negative 
changes, adopt escalation or de-escalation
measures with the issuer;
•The ESG Committee, which brings together all members
of the asset management, the SRI Solutions and the
fundamental analysis teams on a weekly basis during
which the following are carried out: awareness-raising
and monitoring of trends, risks, salient topics  and companies’
human rights development;
•Prioritising 
and  organising enhanced  due diligence  or
engagement, in accordance with the LBP AM's Human
Rights policy.
In addition to these committees, LBP AM relies on a set of
tools and procedures to monitor the effectiveness of its
actions. 
Among them, its proprietary SRI rating methodologies,
which make it possible to incorporate major human
rights risks into its analysis and selection of assets.
These 
methodologies are directly integrated into the
decision-making tools used by the management teams.
These tools make it possible to identify, select and monitor
companies 
and their ability to prevent, mitigate and
remedy the impacts and risks  of human rights impacts.Please  see the glossary  on page 808 for definitions of the main CSR terms 2024 Universal  Registration Document     La Banque Postale 2072Sustainable performance
Social information
Ratings  are included in the management of SRI funds
according to two contribution methodologies to stock
selection. 
These methods tend to disqualify the issuers most
exposed 
to high-impact human rights risks, and favour
those that  best  control  their exposure to these risks:
•Main Adverse Impacts: The SFDR Delegated Regulation
defines a list of indicators to measure the negative impacts
of an issuer  on environmental  and  social  sustainability
factors, known as “IAP indicators”. Among these, indicators
relate  to respect for Human Rights and fundamental
ethical  standards.
•Controversies  monitoring: Data related to data supplier
controversies  makes it possible to monitor issuers, in
particular  their  ability  to prevent and remedy impacts.
•Standards  watchlist:  The standards  watchlist primarily
includes issuers analysed by the GREaT Committee and
marked for monitoring.  This list allows for continuous
monitoring of the issuer and the measures adopted by
the GREaT Committee, as well as their effectiveness,
particularly  in the event of engagement with the
Company.  [S2_4_04]
Severe  human  rights  incidents
As part  of the implementation of its standards-based exclusion
policy, in 2024, LBP AM excluded three companies due to
serious  violations of the fundamental rights of workers in
the supply  chains of  the companies  studied.
As part of  the implementation of its engagement policy,
LBP   AM submitted written questions to the General
Meetings  of two companies, following engagement that
did not sufficiently demonstrate that effective changes
had  been  made  to the  policies and practices  of the  targetcompanies. In both cases, some of the issues were related
to the respect  of fundamental workers’ rights, particularly
in 
supply chains. Following a  serious controversy affecting
a group of companies in the personal care products
sector, LBP AM launched an engagement campaign with
the invested companies covered by this human rights risk.
Several 
individual issuers were  also  subject to more
robust engagement campaigns during 2024, in particular
companies in the automotive and automotive components
sector, to reduce the  risk of severe  human rights impacts
on supply chains. [S2_4_11]
Resources allocated
Remedying La   Banque   Postale 's negative impacts  linked
to the activities of its portfolio companies involves dialogue
with 
customers. If a negative impact is detected through
the controversy management process, La  Banque  Postale
may  ask the business customer to remedy it quickly.
La Banque Postale provides a dedicated team within the
Sustainability 
Department to put its controversy management
process into operation.

Scope
The communities  likely to be affected by significant impacts
related to the  activity  of the  Group and  its subsidiaries or
projects financed through investment or credit activities
are presented in the information published under the
ESRS  2 heading.  [S3_SBM-3_01]
The communities likely to be affected by significant
impacts  are:
•for its own operations, people close to the network, as
part  of La  Banque  Postale Group’s extensive regional
network  and  those covered by societal initiatives;
•for the financed activities,  the communities, including
indigenous peoples, downstream of La Banque Postale
Group’s  value chain, which could be affected  by the
activity of the companies  in the investment portfolio.
[S3_SBM_3_02] [S3_SBM_3_03]
Material impacts,  risks and opportunities
Negative  impacts
The material negative impacts are related to investments
in 
sectors with critical levels of risk, in particular in connection
with operations or materials from conflict zones, risks of
invasion 
of privacy and freedom of expression, environmental
pollution, as well as impacts on  health  and Human Rights.
These  impacts cover La Banque Postale, CNP Assurances,
LBP   AM and Louvre  Banque   Privée, which  have multi-
sectoral investment strategies that are diversified in terms
of 
geographic area. The associated portfolios may therefore
include  companies  with activities  in these  high-risk
sectors.  [S3_SBM_3_04]
Local  and indigenous communities exposed to these
sectors  are particularly vulnerable, especially in the agri-
food,  metals and mining industries, as well as energy  and
utilities (water, gas, renewable energies).  The impacts are
all the more severe for populations with limited access to
remedies, 
such as  indigenous populations, women, children,
displaced populations or those living in conflict or high-
risk areas.
In order to prevent and minimise these negative impacts,
La  Banque  Postale, CNP   Assurances, LBP  AM and
Louvre Banque Privée have adopted responsible investment
strategies.  [S3_SBM_3 _07]
Positive  impacts
La Banque Postale Group’s strategic priorities are aligned
with  those  of the  Caisse  des  Dépôts Group to which it
belongs.  Caisse des  Dépôts Group is a  major public
developer of the French regions and a long-standing financier
of the local public sector. It has three main targets:
economic  development & sovereignty (companies of  all
sizes,  infrastructure),  territorial  cohesion  and  habitat, social
cohesion and  ecological  transformation.La  Banque  Postale’s activities have  positive impacts on
communities. The Group’s extensive network ensures a
presence 
in the regions, providing banking access to
citizens, including in rural or underserved areas.
La Banque Postale’s financing activities also help support
the activities  of local authorities and associations through
dedicated offers. La  Banque  Postale thus participates in
the development of local projects,  such as the renovation
of public  infrastructure, the development  of local services,
ecological  and social initiatives and associative actions in
favour of  inclusion  and  solidarity.
Lastly, societal sponsorship also generates positive impacts.
For example, the L'Envol program, run by La Banque Postale,
supports the education of young people from low-income
backgrounds. In addition, initiatives such as solidarity team
building or the Déclic project aim to raise employee
awareness, engage them in societal projects, and reinforce
the Group’s  impact. For more  information on
La  Banque  Postale Group’s actions and positive impacts,
refer to Section 2.3.3.3 “Commitments to affected
communities  to generate a positive impact”. [S3_SBM_3_05]
Risks and  opportunities
The topic related  to the affected communities is non-
material in La Banque Postale Group's financial materiality
analysis. Indeed, no significant risks or opportunities for
La Banque Postale have been identified in relation to the
affected communities. 
[S3_SBM_3_06]
No significant risk or opportunity was identified for a
specific  group. [S3_SBM 3_08]
